claims.text: The feedstock is cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi high-entropy-alloy powder produced by conventional powder synthesis.
The proposed intervention is controlled in situ substrate pre-heating during additive manufacturing.
Substrate pre-heating reduces the temperature differential and thermal gradient between the molten pool and substrate.
Substrate pre-heating reduces the cooling rate during solidification.
Rapid solidification during additive manufacturing can increase internal stress.
Substrate pre-heating lowers residual stress in additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi.
Substrate pre-heating limits rapid-solidification-induced elemental microsegregation.
Substrate pre-heating reduces microstructural defect formation.
A reduced cooling rate and thermal gradient produce a more uniform grain structure.
A reduced cooling rate and thermal gradient improve phase homogeneity.
A reduced cooling rate and thermal gradient decrease dislocation density at grain boundaries.
The pre-heated thermal environment permits more uniform atomic redistribution during solidification.
Fewer defects and more uniform atomic redistribution improve intergranular cohesion.
Substrate pre-heating improves the mechanical integrity of additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi.
Pre-heated AlCrFeNiSi samples will have higher yield strength than samples additively manufactured without substrate pre-heating.
Pre-heated AlCrFeNiSi samples will have greater ductility than samples additively manufactured without substrate pre-heating.
A substrate temperature around 600–700 °C can moderate cooling without inducing unwanted phase changes.
The hypothesis applies to substrate-heatable additive-manufacturing methods such as selective laser melting and directed energy deposition.
The optimal substrate pre-heating temperature is alloy- and machine-specific.
Failure to obtain statistically significant reductions in residual stress and segregation defects together with improved mechanical performance would falsify the hypothesis.
